**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0760), Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections. All the questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Regle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each of the sections » (3 sections : A 1800-1922, B 1922-1961, C 1961 to present, 4 questions chacune, numerotation continue 1 a 12). `regles_choix` porte le minimum impose, une regle `parmi 1 sur 4` par section ; la regle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable et est recopiee dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « (25 marks) » et la page de garde dit « All the questions carry equal marks » ; `points` de l'exercice et de la question unique valent 25. Aucun ecart avec le sujet (4 x 25 = 100).

Defauts d'impression du sujet : scan de deux pages (CamScanner) avec filigrane gcerevision.com et bandeau publicitaire, sans incidence sur la lecture, mais avec une legere transparence de texte (verso) en haut de la page 2 et entre quelques questions ; les intitules de section sont imprimes avec un tiret demi-cadratin (« 1800 - 1922 ») recopie avec un tiret simple ; la question 2 est imprimee « succeed to extend » (tournure incorrecte, recopiee telle quelle) ; la question 3 est ambigue (« the results of German annexation by 1884 ») ; la question 6 est maladroite (« indigenous resistance and failure against French rule »). Aucune figure, carte ni document dans le sujet. Page de garde verifiee : ADVANCED LEVEL, History 2, Paper 2 - Cameroon History Since 1800, code 0760, JUNE 2026 (reference GCE26/0760/2/BN).

Aucun corrige officiel : les corriges sont des reponses modeles redigees de memoire, sans acces a une source. Les dates, noms et traites sont ceux de l'historiographie etablie ; les faits dont la precision est moindre sont formules prudemment ou sans chiffre. Aucune citation, statistique ni source n'est inventee. Les corriges sont a relire par un historien du Cameroun avant diffusion.

Question 5 : les details chiffres et locaux (dates d'ouverture de routes, d'ecoles, d'hopitaux, noms de plantations) ne sont pas donnes ; le corrige s'en tient a l'ordre en conseil de 1923 (administration avec le Nigeria), a la vente aux encheres des plantations allemandes dans les annees 1920 (rachat en grande partie par d'anciens proprietaires allemands et par Lever Brothers), a la creation du St Joseph's College de Sasse (1939) et a la Cameroons Development Corporation (1946), qui releve de la tutelle et non du mandat. La part respective de chaque mission dans l'education n'est pas precisee. A faire relire par un historien du Cameroun si diffusion.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Critically examine the contributions of the British administration to the socio-economic development of Southern Cameroons during the Mandate period.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** After the First World War the League of Nations gave Britain a mandate over part of the former German Kamerun. The British Cameroons were divided into a northern part and a southern part and, under an Order in Council of 1923, were administered as part of Nigeria (the Southern Cameroons together with the southern provinces of Nigeria and, later, with its Eastern Provinces). Under the Covenant of the League the mandatory was supposed to promote the "material and moral well-being" of the inhabitants. "Critically examine" means weighing what Britain really contributed against its limits. The period covered is 1922 to 1946, when the mandate was replaced by a UN trusteeship.

**1. The contributions.**
(a) *Peace and an administrative framework.* Britain brought an end to the First World War disruptions and set up a stable administration based on divisions and Native Authorities under the system of indirect rule, with native courts and treasuries, and chiefs as intermediaries. This system gave local people some experience of local government.
(b) *Plantation agriculture.* The former German plantations around Mount Cameroon were taken over and, from the early 1920s, sold at auction; many were bought back by former German owners and others went to companies such as Lever Brothers. They produced bananas, rubber, palm products and cocoa for export, gave wage employment and gave the territory some exports and revenue.
(c) *Cash crops by small farmers.* Cocoa, palm products and, in the Grassfields, coffee and other crops were encouraged on smallholdings, and marketing and trade developed.
(d) *Communications.* Roads, bridges, paths and ports (Tiko and Victoria, now Limbe, for exports) were built or improved to link plantations and towns such as Kumba, Mamfe and Bamenda, often with communal labour from the Native Authorities. Telegraph and postal services were extended.
(e) *Education and health through the missions.* The administration left most schooling to the missions (Basel Mission, which was allowed back in the 1920s, Catholic missions, Baptists and others), giving them small grants. Mission and government schools and, in 1939, St Joseph's College at Sasse produced the first clerks, teachers and leaders. Government and mission hospitals, dispensaries and campaigns against sleeping sickness and other diseases were set up.
(f) *Legal order and wage labour.* A court system, police and labour regulations were introduced; towns, markets and wage labour developed.

**2. The limits and failures.**
(a) *Administration as a part of Nigeria.* The territory was treated as a remote appendage of Nigeria, with little separate planning and few funds. Its budget was small and policy was decided in Lagos and later in Enugu, far from the territory.
(b) *Little investment.* Indirect rule was cheap and the British spent little. There was almost no industry and no processing of raw materials; the economy remained dependent on the export of a few raw materials.
(c) *Plantation economy at local expense.* Land taken by the Germans was not returned to the Bakweri, who were left with insufficient land (a problem raised repeatedly and studied by commissions of enquiry), and plantation workers, many of them migrants from Nigeria, were poorly paid and housed.
(d) *Weak education.* The missions provided most schooling; secondary education was scarce until very late, higher education did not exist, and literacy remained low. Few Cameroonians reached senior posts.
(e) *Poor infrastructure.* Roads were basic and the Grassfields remained poorly linked; towns were small.
(f) *Dependence on Nigerians.* Nigerian (especially Igbo) traders, clerks and labourers dominated much of the commerce and the lower civil service, so local people benefited less.
(g) *Cultural and political marginalisation.* Southern Cameroons had no real political voice until the 1940s and 1950s. Reports to the League's Permanent Mandates Commission frequently praised progress while the real work was limited.

**3. Assessment.** Britain's contribution was real but modest: peace, a legal and administrative framework, some cash-crop expansion, basic transport and the beginnings of schools and health services, mostly through missions and plantations. The administration invested little and used the territory mainly as an extension of Nigeria. The major development initiatives, such as the Cameroons Development Corporation (1946), the expansion of education and the move toward self-government, came after the Second World War and the arrival of the trusteeship system.

**Conclusion.** The British administration contributed to the socio-economic development of Southern Cameroons by providing order, local administration, an export economy, basic communications and a start in education and health, but these contributions were limited by indirect rule, cheap administration, attachment to Nigeria and the priorities of plantations and missions. The territory remained underdeveloped at the end of the Mandate.
